title: Twelve Monkeys
events_chronological: A virus released in the mid-nineteen-nineties kills most of the human race and drives the survivors underground.
Decades later the scientists running the underground colony send convicts up to collect specimens, and James Cole volunteers.
Cole is sent back in time, arrives six years too early, and is arrested raving about a plague.
In the asylum the psychiatrist Kathryn Railly interviews Cole, and he meets Jeffrey Goines, the son of a famous virologist.
Cole is pulled back to the future and interrogated about a voicemail recording the scientists have recovered.
Cole is sent to the right year and abducts Railly, who has since written a book about apocalyptic prophecy.
Cole and Railly find graffiti for the Army of the Twelve Monkeys and trace Goines to his father's estate.
Goines denies everything and says the idea of stealing the virus was Cole's own, from the asylum.
Railly comes across a photograph from the First World War of a soldier who is unmistakably Cole.
Cole decides he has been insane all along and asks to be allowed to stay where he is.
Railly finds a bullet fired in 1917 in an X-ray of Cole and understands that he has been telling the truth.
The Army of the Twelve Monkeys turn out to be animal rights activists who release the zoo animals and shut Goines's father in a cupboard.
Cole and Railly go to the airport in disguise to stop the virologist's assistant, who is the real carrier.
Railly spots the carrier, Cole runs at him with a gun, and airport police shoot Cole dead while a small boy watches from the concourse.
The carrier boards his flight with the virus, seated beside one of the scientists from the future.
syuzhet_notes: The film opens on a fragment of the airport shooting and returns to it as a dream throughout, without the audience or the protagonist being able to place it. Only in the last minutes is it shown whole and revealed as his own death, watched by himself as a child.
fabula_notes: The dream and the ending are one event, counted once here at its chronological position near the end. Everything else runs forward, including the jumps between the two periods, which are the protagonist's own sequence.
